newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila meeting voices concern over Burma, China.
newsitem.headline: Manila meeting voices concern over Burma, China.

text.p: Security experts voiced concern over any hasty admission of Burma to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) as they ended an international conference in Manila on Tuesday, a conference official said.

Other anxieties expressed by delegates ranged from China's intentions if it became a superpower to political succession in that country and in Indonesia, Carolina Hernandez, president of the Philippine Institute for Strategic Studies and Development Studies, said.
The two-day meeting, co-sponsored by the institute and Germany's Konrad Adenauer Foundation, was attended by officials, academics and scholars from 12 countries.
Hernandez said the view of a majority of non-governmental experts was that "they recognised the need for one Southeast Asia at some future time but it need not be now."
Burma, along with Laos and Cambodia, has applied for admission to ASEAN, which groups Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Singapore, the Philippines, Vietnam and Brunei.
ASEAN leaders at a summit in Jakarta last weekend agreed to simultaneously admit the three but did not say when.
Hernandez said the experts believed simultaneous admissions would disadvantage ASEAN.

"It is possible that Laos and Cambodia could be sidelined or left out... because Burma is a bigger, more strategic country. You might give an inordinate attention to Burma, in a sense deflecting external criticisms," she told reporters.
The United States and other Western countries have slammed Burma for its human rights record. Their attacks have intensified following Rangoon's renewed crackdown on pro-democracy activists.
Hernandez said the experts believed Burma's admission now could also create difficulties for ASEAN in its dealings with Western dialogue partners, some of whom are also its major trading partners.
Several experts also voiced concern at political succession in Indonesia and China, pointing out that succession was always a problem in countries whose leaders have been in power for some time.
An emergent China was also a source of concern.

"One scenario is China behaves so badly or refuses to cooperate, then the countries in the region will probably have no alternative but to get together to defend themselves," Hernandez said. "But everyone has a scenario...(it) is like a game."
Ambassador Yang Chengxu, president of the China Institute of International Relations, tried to allay fears about his country, saying people overestimated China's strength.
"The aim of certain major powers in creating the fallacy of China's threat is to deliberately drive a wedge between China and the medium and small-sized nations in this region," he said.
Political turmoil or economic crisis in China could affect Asia's stability but the country's rise as a superpower should not worry its neighbours, Yang said.
